subtopics.name: Discharge planning and continuity of care

questions.stem: A nurse in a cardiology clinic has four telephone messages to return at the start of the afternoon. Which call should the nurse return first?

options.text: A client discharged 3 days ago with heart failure who has gained 2.5 kg (5.5 lb) in 2 days and now sleeps sitting up in a chair
A client taking warfarin who forgot yesterday's dose and wants to know whether to take two tablets today to catch up
A client with stable angina who wants to know whether a new over-the-counter cold medicine containing pseudoephedrine is safe to take
A client who started insulin last week and asks how long an opened pen can be kept at room temperature before it should be thrown away

rationale.correct: When returning calls, start with the client whose symptoms suggest an acute, worsening physiological problem.

perOption.a: Rapid weight gain with orthopnea signals worsening fluid overload and possible pulmonary edema; this client may need urgent care today.
perOption.b: A missed warfarin dose needs advice, but it is not urgent; doubling is not advised, and the call can follow the more unstable client.
perOption.c: Decongestants can raise blood pressure, but this question can wait briefly.
perOption.d: Storage questions matter but are not urgent.

questions.educationalObjective: Prioritize telephone calls.

questions.stem: A provider prescribes IV metoprolol 5 mg now for a client whose heart rate is 48/min and blood pressure is 86/50 mm Hg. The nurse questions the order, and the provider says, "Just give it. I know what I'm doing." What should the nurse do next?

options.text: Give the dose as prescribed and document that the provider was told about the vital signs
Hold the dose and notify the charge nurse or nursing supervisor about the disagreement
Give half the dose and recheck the heart rate and blood pressure in 15 minutes
Ask the pharmacist to change the prescription to a lower dose before giving it

rationale.correct: A nurse is accountable for every dose given. If a prescription seems unsafe and the provider will not change it, hold the drug and go up the chain of command.

perOption.a: Documenting a concern does not make it safe to give a drug that can worsen bradycardia and hypotension.
perOption.b: The nurse must not give a dose likely to harm the client and should use the chain of command to resolve the conflict.
perOption.c: Changing a dose without a prescription is outside the nurse's scope and still risks harm.
perOption.d: A pharmacist can advise, but cannot overrule the provider; the nursing chain of command is the next step.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Use the chain of command for an unsafe prescription.

questions.stem: A nurse educator is reviewing ethical principles with new graduates. For each nursing action, indicate the ethical principle it best shows.

rows.text: Supporting a client's informed decision to stop dialysis
Returning at 1400 as promised to help a client practice walking
Giving the same pain assessment and care to an unhoused client as to every other client
Turning a client every 2 hours to prevent a pressure injury

rationale.correct: Autonomy: respecting choices. Beneficence: doing good. Justice: fairness. Fidelity: keeping promises.

perOption.r1:c1: Respecting a competent client's own choice is autonomy.
perOption.r1:c2: Beneficence is acting for the client's good; here the nurse is respecting the client's choice.
perOption.r1:c3: Justice is about fair distribution of care.
perOption.r2:c1: The action is about keeping a commitment, not the client's choice.
perOption.r2:c2: It benefits the client, but the key point is keeping one's word.
perOption.r2:c3: Fairness among clients is not the issue.
perOption.r2:c4: Keeping a promise made to a client is fidelity.
perOption.r3:c1: The client's choice is not the issue.
perOption.r3:c2: Doing good is involved, but the key point is equal treatment.
perOption.r3:c3: Fair, equal care regardless of social status is justice.
perOption.r4:c1: The action is not about a choice the client made.
perOption.r4:c2: Acting to benefit the client and prevent harm is beneficence.
perOption.r4:c3: Fair distribution is not the issue.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify ethical principles in nursing actions.

questions.stem: A 34-year-old client on a ventilator after a motorcycle crash has been declared dead by neurological criteria. The family is at the bedside, and no one has mentioned organ donation. Facility policy follows federal regulations. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the family whether they would consider donating the client's organs
Notify the organ procurement organization about the death as policy requires
Wait to see whether the family raises the subject of donation on their own
Check the client's driver's license and tell the family about any donor status

rationale.correct: Every death or imminent death is referred to the organ procurement organization, whose trained staff approach the family about donation.

perOption.a: Requests are best made by trained requesters from the organ procurement organization, which leads to better family decisions.
perOption.b: Hospitals must refer every death or imminent death to the organ procurement organization, which decides suitability and approaches the family.
perOption.c: Waiting does not meet the required referral and may lose the chance to honor the client's wishes.
perOption.d: Donor registration is confirmed and discussed by the organ procurement organization, not the bedside nurse.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Follow the organ donation referral process.

questions.stem: An unconscious client's durable power of attorney for health care names the client's sister as decision-maker. The sister asks that the client not be placed on a ventilator, as the client wished. The client's spouse insists that "everything be done." What should the nurse do?

options.text: Follow the spouse's wishes, because a spouse is the legal next of kin
Support the sister's decision and notify the provider about the family conflict
Delay any decision about the ventilator until the spouse and the sister both agree with each other
Ask the hospital lawyer to choose which family member's wishes to follow

rationale.correct: A health care agent named in a durable power of attorney makes decisions for the client when the client cannot, ahead of other family members.

perOption.a: A valid durable power of attorney for health care takes priority over next of kin.
perOption.b: The named agent speaks for the client; the nurse supports that decision and gets the provider involved, often with an ethics or palliative care consult.
perOption.c: Waiting for agreement can override the client's wishes and the legal agent.
perOption.d: The legal document already names the decision-maker.

questions.educationalObjective: Follow a durable power of attorney for health care.

questions.stem: A nurse manager is reviewing staff social media posts after a complaint. Which posts violate client confidentiality? Select all that apply.

options.text: A selfie at the nurses' station with the client assignment board visible in the background
"Long night caring for a famous singer in room 412. They were so nice!"
"Proud to be a nurse. Twelve hours done on a busy unit, and I'd do it all again tomorrow."
A photo of a healing wound posted without the client's face, shared in a private group of nurses
A link to the hospital's public press release about the new cardiac unit opening next month

rationale.correct: Nothing that could identify a client, including images, room numbers or details, may be shared on social media, even in private groups.

perOption.a: Client names on the board are protected information, even if they are only in the background.
perOption.b: The details could identify the client, even without a name.
perOption.c: This post shares no client information.
perOption.d: Images of clients shared without consent are a privacy breach, and private groups are not secure.
perOption.e: Public information about the facility does not involve clients.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Identify social media confidentiality breaches.

questions.stem: A client who is recovering from pneumonia asks the nurse, "Can I read what's in my chart? I want to know what the doctors wrote about me." What is the nurse's best response?

options.text: "Medical records belong to the hospital, so they are kept for the staff who care for you."
"You have the right to see your record. I'll find out how our facility arranges that."
"Your doctor will need to approve that request in writing before anyone can show the chart to you."
"Why do you want to read it? Is there something you're worried about?"

rationale.correct: Clients have the right to see and obtain copies of their health records; follow the facility's procedure.

perOption.a: Clients have a legal right to see and get copies of their own records.
perOption.b: Clients may access their records; the nurse follows the facility's process, which often includes someone to explain the entries.
perOption.c: Access is a client right and is not up to the provider's approval.
perOption.d: Exploring worries can be useful, but "why" questions sound defensive and do not answer the request.

questions.stem: After surgery was performed on the wrong knee, the hospital starts a root cause analysis. Which statement by the nurse manager to the team best reflects the purpose of a root cause analysis?

options.text: "We need to find out which person made the mistake so that they can be retrained."
"We'll look at every step and system that allowed this to happen, not just who was involved."
"The surgeon is responsible for marking the site, so this review is about the surgeon."
"Since no lasting harm occurred to the client, we can keep this review short and close the case quickly."

rationale.correct: A root cause analysis is a non-punitive review of the systems and processes behind a serious event, aimed at preventing it from happening again.

perOption.a: Focusing on one person misses the system failures that let the error happen.
perOption.b: Root cause analysis looks for system and process failures and fixes them to prevent the same error.
perOption.c: Wrong-site surgery involves many checks and people; blaming one role misses system causes.
perOption.d: Wrong-site surgery is a sentinel event that needs full review whether or not lasting harm occurred.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.stem: The electronic health record and the barcode medication system go offline for planned maintenance for 4 hours. A client is due a scheduled dose of IV vancomycin during that time. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Delay the dose until the system is back online so it can be scanned and documented
Give the dose using the printed medication record and the facility's downtime procedure
Give the dose and keep a note on scrap paper to enter later from memory
Ask the provider to change the vancomycin to an oral antibiotic until the system is restored

rationale.correct: During EHR downtime, follow the downtime procedure: printed medication records, manual identity checks and official paper documentation entered later.

perOption.a: Delaying a timed antibiotic can reduce its effect; downtime procedures allow safe care to continue.
perOption.b: Downtime procedures use printed records and manual checks, with entries added to the electronic record once it is restored.
perOption.c: Informal notes are not secure and risk errors; the official downtime forms are used.
perOption.d: There is no clinical reason to change therapy because of planned downtime.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Provide safe care during system downtime.

questions.stem: An off-duty nurse stops at the scene of a car crash and finds an adult who is breathing, conscious and bleeding heavily from a forearm wound. Emergency medical services have been called. Which action best protects the client and the nurse legally?

options.text: Apply direct pressure to the wound and stay with the client until EMS takes over care
Drive the client to the nearest hospital in the nurse's own car to save time
Leave once the bleeding slows, since the nurse is not on duty and EMS has been called and is on the way
Give the client a pain pill from the nurse's own supply to keep them calm

rationale.correct: Good Samaritan protection covers reasonable emergency care within one's training, given without pay, until care is handed to equal or higher-level responders.

perOption.a: Good Samaritan laws protect reasonable care within the nurse's training; once care starts, the nurse stays until someone equally or more qualified takes over.
perOption.b: Moving and transporting the client is outside reasonable first aid and could cause harm.
perOption.c: Leaving after starting care could be abandonment.
perOption.d: Giving medication without a prescription is outside the scope of emergency aid.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Apply Good Samaritan principles.

questions.stem: A staff nurse who is 20 weeks pregnant is working on an oncology unit. Which client should the charge nurse avoid assigning to this nurse?

options.text: A client receiving oral capecitabine for colon cancer who needs help with meal planning
A client with a sealed cesium implant for cervical cancer that was placed this morning
A client with neutropenia after chemotherapy who is on protective precautions
A client with metastatic breast cancer who needs teaching about a new pain regimen

rationale.correct: Pregnant staff should not care for clients with sealed internal radiation sources and should avoid other high-risk exposures as policy directs.

perOption.a: The nurse can use precautions with oral chemotherapy, and meal planning involves no special exposure.
perOption.b: Internal radiation sources expose staff to radiation; pregnant staff should not care for these clients.
perOption.c: Neutropenic precautions protect the client and pose no special risk to a pregnant nurse.
perOption.d: Pain teaching carries no special exposure risk.

questions.stem: A nurse calls a provider about a client whose oxygen saturation has fallen. Place the parts of the SBAR report in the order the nurse should give them.

items.text: "The client is 2 days after a colectomy and has a history of COPD; SpO2 was 94% this morning."
"This is the nurse on 5 West calling about the client in room 8, who has an SpO2 of 86% on 2 L/min."
"Respirations are 30/min with crackles on the right; I'm concerned about pneumonia."
"I'd like you to come and see the client, and I recommend a chest x-ray."

rationale.correct: SBAR: situation, background, assessment, recommendation. It gives the provider the key facts in a predictable order.

perOption.a: Situation: who is calling and what is happening now.
perOption.b: Background: the relevant history and baseline.
perOption.c: Assessment: the nurse's findings and interpretation.
perOption.d: Recommendation: what the nurse is asking for.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Give an SBAR report.

questions.stem: During discharge medication reconciliation, the nurse sees that a client's home list includes metformin 1,000 mg twice daily, but the discharge prescriptions do not mention metformin and the record gives no reason. The client's last creatinine was normal. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Tell the client to keep taking metformin at home as before
Tell the client to stop metformin, since it is not on the new list
Contact the provider to clarify whether metformin should be continued
Discharge the client and ask the primary care provider to sort it out at follow-up

rationale.correct: Medication reconciliation compares all medicines at each transition; any unexplained difference must be clarified with the provider.

perOption.a: The nurse cannot decide to continue a drug that was left off the discharge plan.
perOption.b: Stopping a diabetes drug without a known reason could cause hyperglycemia.
perOption.c: An unexplained discrepancy between home and discharge medicines must be clarified before discharge.
perOption.d: Leaving the discrepancy for later risks harm in the meantime.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Resolve a discrepancy during medication reconciliation.

questions.stem: An assistive personnel (AP) reports that a client who walked in the hall 10 minutes ago now has a blood pressure of 88/50 mm Hg. It was 128/76 mm Hg this morning. The client is 1 day after a bowel resection. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Ask the AP to recheck the blood pressure with a manual cuff in 15 minutes and report the result to the nurse
Go to assess the client right away, including heart rate, dressing and level of consciousness
Tell the AP to have the client stay in bed and drink a large glass of water
Document the reading and tell the provider at the next scheduled rounds

rationale.correct: AP collect data; the RN assesses and acts on abnormal findings. An unexpected change in vital signs needs the nurse at the bedside.

perOption.a: A large drop needs the nurse's assessment now; delegating a recheck delays care.
perOption.b: An unexpected drop in blood pressure after surgery may be bleeding or hypovolemia and needs RN assessment at once.
perOption.c: Fluids by mouth are not a treatment for possible hemorrhage, and the client needs assessment.
perOption.d: Waiting for rounds could let a serious problem progress.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Act on data reported by assistive personnel.

questions.stem: The nurse is reviewing clients on a medical unit. For which 2 clients should the nurse call the rapid response team?

options.text: A client with pneumonia whose respiratory rate is now 32/min and SpO2 is 88% on 4 L/min
A client with a new urinary tract infection who has a temperature of 38.2 °C (100.8 °F) and is alert
A client who suddenly cannot find words and has a facial droop that started 20 minutes ago
A client with chronic kidney disease whose potassium is 5.3 mEq/L and who has no ECG changes
A client after a knee replacement who rates pain 8 of 10 an hour after an oral opioid

rationale.correct: Call the rapid response team for acute changes such as worsening breathing, new neurological deficits, hypotension or sudden changes in consciousness.

perOption.a: Rising work of breathing with low oxygen despite oxygen is a rapid response trigger.
perOption.b: A low fever in an alert client can be managed by the nurse and provider.
perOption.c: Sudden neurological deficits suggest a stroke; rapid response speeds stroke care.
perOption.d: Mild hyperkalemia without ECG changes is reported to the provider, not a rapid response emergency.
perOption.e: Uncontrolled pain needs provider contact but is not a rapid response trigger.

questions.educationalObjective: Decide when to call the rapid response team.

questions.stem: Before witnessing the consent for a colonoscopy, the nurse talks with the client. Highlight the client statements that show the consent may not be informed or voluntary.

segments.text: "The doctor explained it, but I didn't really follow the part about a perforation."
"I finished the bowel prep last night."
"My son says I have to do this or he won't help me anymore."
"I know they'll give me medicine to make me sleepy."
"I'm not sure what else they could do instead."

rationale.correct: Informed consent needs understanding of the procedure, risks, benefits and alternatives, and a voluntary decision; gaps are reported to the provider before signing.

perOption.s2: The client does not understand a key risk, so consent is not yet informed.
perOption.s4: This is preparation, not a consent concern.
perOption.s6: Pressure from family suggests the decision may not be voluntary.
perOption.s8: The client understands sedation will be used.
perOption.s10: The client does not know the alternatives, which are part of informed consent.

questions.educationalObjective: Recognize problems with informed consent.

questions.stem: The spouse of a client who was just diagnosed with pancreatic cancer asks the nurse, "Please don't tell my spouse it's cancer. It will destroy them." The client is alert and has asked twice what the biopsy showed. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Agree to keep the diagnosis from the client to protect them from distress
Tell the client the diagnosis now, before the spouse can stop the provider from sharing it
Explore the spouse's fears, explain the client's right to know, and involve the provider
Tell the spouse the decision belongs to the provider, and do nothing further

rationale.correct: Competent clients have the right to truthful information about their own health. Support the family's fears, but do not withhold the truth from a client who wants it.

perOption.a: Withholding a diagnosis from a competent client who asks violates veracity and autonomy.
perOption.b: The provider shares a new diagnosis; acting alone without the team or exploring the spouse's fears is not appropriate.
perOption.c: The nurse acknowledges the spouse's concern while upholding the client's right to information and works with the provider on how to share it.
perOption.d: This avoids the ethical issue and leaves the spouse without support.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment

questions.educationalObjective: Balance veracity with family wishes.

questions.stem: Which situation requires the nurse to complete an incident report?

options.text: A client refuses the evening dose of a stool softener
A visitor slips on a wet floor in the client's room and hurts a wrist
A client's blood glucose before lunch is 245 mg/dL and insulin is given late
A client is discharged home 1 day earlier than the team had planned

rationale.correct: Incident reports record unusual events that harm or could harm clients, visitors or staff, such as falls, errors and injuries.

perOption.a: A refusal is documented in the record, not as an incident.
perOption.b: Injuries to visitors are unusual occurrences that must be reported.
perOption.c: An abnormal finding is reported to the provider and charted, not an incident.
perOption.d: Early discharge is a care decision, not an incident.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Identify events that need an incident report.

questions.stem: While buying lunch in the hospital cafeteria, the nurse finds a printed unit census sheet with client names, room numbers and diagnoses left on a table. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Throw the sheet into the nearest cafeteria trash can right away
Take the sheet, place it in a secure shred bin and report the breach as policy requires
Leave the sheet where it is, since the person who left it will come back for it
Post a photo of the sheet in the unit's staff group chat so the nurse who lost it can come and collect it

rationale.correct: Protected health information found in public must be secured, disposed of securely and reported under facility policy.

perOption.a: Ordinary trash is not secure; client information must be shredded or placed in secure disposal.
perOption.b: Securing the information and reporting the possible breach protects clients and allows follow-up.
perOption.c: Leaving it allows anyone to read protected information.
perOption.d: Photographing and sharing client information spreads the breach.

references: NCSBN National Guidelines for Nursing Delegation; LaCharity, Prioritization, Delegation & Assignment
Written to NCLEX-RN difficulty and reviewed by the content team on 20 November 2026.

questions.educationalObjective: Respond to a breach of client information.

questions.stem: After a suspected bioterrorism event, a client is admitted with fever, chest pain and a widened mediastinum on chest x-ray. Inhalation anthrax is suspected. Which precautions should the nurse use?

options.text: Airborne precautions in a negative-pressure room with an N95 respirator
Standard precautions, because inhalation anthrax does not spread between people
Droplet precautions with a surgical mask within 2 m (6 ft) of the client
Contact precautions with a gown and gloves for any care given inside the client's room

rationale.correct: Inhalation anthrax needs only standard precautions; smallpox needs airborne and contact, and plague (pneumonic) needs droplet precautions.

perOption.a: Inhalation anthrax is not spread from person to person, so airborne precautions are not needed.
perOption.b: Anthrax spores infect people from the environment; once in the body, inhalation anthrax does not spread from client to client.
perOption.c: Inhalation anthrax does not spread by droplets.
perOption.d: Contact precautions are added only for draining cutaneous lesions, not inhalation anthrax.

questions.stem: A client has a sealed radioactive implant for cervical cancer. During morning care, the nurse sees the implant lying in the bed linens. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Pick it up with a gloved hand and put it back in the client's vagina
Use long-handled forceps to place it in the lead container in the room
Wrap it in the bed linens and send them to the laundry immediately
Leave it where it is and ask the client to move to another bed until help arrives

rationale.correct: A dislodged sealed source is handled only with long-handled forceps and placed in the lead container; notify radiation safety and the provider.

perOption.a: The nurse should not touch the source by hand or reinsert it.
perOption.b: Distance and shielding protect staff; the source goes in the lead container and radiation safety is notified.
perOption.c: This would expose laundry staff and lose the source.
perOption.d: Leaving the source exposed continues the radiation exposure.

questions.stem: The nurse is teaching the parents of a 14-month-old child about home safety. Which instructions should the nurse include? Select all that apply.

options.text: Set the water heater to 49 °C (120 °F) or lower
Keep medicines and cleaning products locked up and out of reach
Use a baby walker so the child can move around safely
Install safety gates at the top and bottom of stairs
Anchor tall furniture and televisions to the wall
Give whole grapes and nuts as healthy finger foods

rationale.correct: Toddler safety: lower water temperature, locked poisons, gates, anchored furniture and no choking-hazard foods or walkers.

perOption.a: Lower water temperature prevents scald burns.
perOption.b: Toddlers explore by putting things in their mouths, so poisoning is a major risk.
perOption.c: Baby walkers cause falls down stairs and are not recommended.
perOption.d: Gates prevent falls, a leading cause of toddler injury.
perOption.e: Tip-over injuries happen when toddlers climb furniture.
perOption.f: Round, firm foods are choking hazards for toddlers.

references: Pediatric nursing texts (e.g. Hockenberry, Wong's Essentials of Pediatric Nursing)

questions.educationalObjective: Teach toddler home safety.

questions.stem: The nurse is assisting in the operating room before a right inguinal hernia repair. During the time-out, the consent form says "right" but the site marking is on the left groin. What should the nurse do?

options.text: Proceed, since the consent form is the legal document that decides the side
Stop the time-out and ask that the procedure not start until the mismatch is resolved
Wipe off the marking and redraw it on the right side to match the consent
Note the discrepancy in an incident report after the surgery is finished and the client is in recovery

rationale.correct: The universal protocol: pre-procedure verification, site marking and a time-out in which any team member can stop the procedure if something does not match.

perOption.a: Any mismatch during the time-out must be resolved before the procedure starts.
perOption.b: The universal protocol lets any team member stop the procedure until the correct site is confirmed with the client and records.
perOption.c: The surgeon marks the site with the client's involvement; the nurse does not change it.
perOption.d: Reporting afterward does not prevent wrong-site surgery.

questions.educationalObjective: Apply the universal protocol.

questions.stem: A client in the emergency department is pacing, clenching their fists and shouting that they have waited too long. The client steps toward the nurse and says, "Somebody is going to get hurt." What should the nurse do first?

options.text: Tell the client firmly that threats will not be tolerated and they must sit down now
Stand between the client and the door so the client cannot leave the department
Keep a clear path to the exit, call for help and speak calmly in short sentences
Turn away and give the client space by going to the back of the room alone

rationale.correct: With an escalating client: keep a clear exit, call for help early, keep a safe distance and use calm, simple language.

perOption.a: A confrontational tone can escalate aggression.
perOption.b: Blocking the exit traps both the nurse and the client and increases danger.
perOption.c: The nurse protects their own safety, gets help early and uses calm de-escalation.
perOption.d: Turning away and isolating oneself leaves the nurse unable to watch the client or get out.
